questions.q: What is the grain of silver.sales_transactions, and why does that matter for counting orders in Gold?
options: One row per store; order count has no relationship to line items
One row per calendar day; counting rows and counting orders are always identical
One row per customer; line items are irrelevant to the order count
One row per sale line item; a single order with multiple line items would be over-counted by a plain count(order_id)
questions.explain: Because Silver has one row per line item, a single three-item order produces three rows sharing the same order_id, so a naive row count would inflate the order count.

questions.q: Why does this lesson use countDistinct("order_id") instead of count("order_id")?
options: count("order_id") is not valid PySpark syntax
countDistinct counts each unique order once regardless of how many line items it had, which is what order count is supposed to mean
countDistinct is faster to execute on every dataset size
count("order_id") only works on string columns, not integer IDs
questions.explain: count(order_id) would count line items, not orders, inflating the number for any order with more than one product on it.

questions.q: In the PySpark aggregation code, why is sum imported as `from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum`?
options: Because sum is also a Python built-in function, and aliasing avoids shadowing it
Because PySpark does not have a function named sum
Because Delta tables require all aggregate functions to have an underscore prefix
Because _sum runs faster than sum in Spark's execution engine
questions.explain: Importing sum directly would shadow Python's own built-in sum() function in that notebook, so it's commonly aliased to _sum.

questions.q: What does the Spark SQL CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT statement in this lesson accomplish?
options: The identical aggregation as the PySpark groupBy/agg version, written as SQL against the same Silver table
A command that only works on streaming DataFrames, not batch tables
A way to delete the Bronze table permanently
A completely different aggregation that ignores sale_date
questions.explain: CTAS is the SQL equivalent of writing a DataFrame's grouped result to a new table — both versions in this lesson produce the same gold.daily_sales_summary.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call .orderBy("sale_date") before writing the Gold table, even though it isn't required for correctness?
options: Delta tables will refuse to write unsorted data
orderBy is required for countDistinct to function correctly
It makes the table easier to spot-check by eye while building and validating the pipeline, even though Delta doesn't guarantee on-disk row order anyway
Sorting reduces the number of rows in the final table
questions.explain: Sorting is a convenience for readability during development and validation, not a correctness requirement for the aggregation itself.
